pOne: To put it simply, the difference between the two domains is respectively what you're trying to measure: what kind of analysis you are trying to perform. You should make an effort to use the methods that are most suitable for your study, but both hold advantages that can compliment each other. When speaking in the time domain, you have an element of time. A good example of time domain analysis is the spectrogram. The spectrogram is a three-dimension graph that measures the power of frequencies across a span of time.
pTwo: In direct contrast, the frequency domain is only concerned with overall power when talking about EEG systems. We only care about the frequency contents and the bands of interest. The element of time does not preside or make statements about the data. The most standard EEG example of the frequency domain is the power spectral density plot (PSD). This plot measures the overall power of frequency features with respect to each electrode. In most cases, this is done with welch's method but other methods can be used. It may be helpful to learn more about the discrete fourier transformation and some signal processing basics at this stage, but it is not required.
pThree:
The five frequency bands are known sequentially as Delta (0-4 Hz), Theta (4-8 Hz), Alpha (8-12 Hz), Beta(12-30 Hz), and Gamma (30+ Hz). Each band can describe a person's level of alertness or focus. Large sums of delta are associated with deep sleep, Theta with light sleep, and Alpha with meditative or drowsy states of mind. Beta and Gamma are more alert states associated with critical thinking and focus. 
It really should be stated that there is some scholarly debate on which ranges pertain exactly to each type of wave, but these ranges are generally accepted and are incredibly varied with what they tell us about the human state. We can extract more information than just alertness from EEG frequency bands as they relate to certain lobes of the brain.
